Cryptography is the science of reading and writing coded messages. It is the fundamental component of the mechanisms for:

  • Authentication: establishes the identity of the sender and the receiver.
  • Integrity: ensures the data was not altered.
  • Confidentiality: nobody except the sender and the receiver can intercept the data.
  • Non-repudiation (binding): ties a document or transaction to a person or a system.
Each technique in this lesson covers one or more of these four goals.

In general, a cryptographic mechanism uses an algorithm and a key.

The key space is the range of possible key values. The larger it is, the harder it is to obtain the key by brute force: trying every possible combination until it is found.

With an n-bit key there are 2ⁿ values: each bit added doubles the attacker's work.
Security rests on the size of the key space.
Brute force: trying one key after another until the right one is found. With 8 bits that is 256 attempts; with 128 bits it is impractical.

Also called secret key encryption: it uses a single shared key and the same algorithm to encrypt and to decrypt.

It is the most efficient in terms of computation. Its complication is key distribution: both ends must have the same key, without anyone else knowing it.

Examples: DES, 3DES (triple DES), RC4, IDEA, and AES (128/192/256).
secret key K · same at both ends
The problem is not the algorithm but the key: how does it reach B without anyone else seeing it?

This is public key encryption. Instead of a single key, a pair is generated: the public key is made known and the private key is kept secret.

Data is encrypted with the recipient's public key and decrypted with their private key. Each party gives the other their public key.

It requires more computation than symmetric encryption. It is used for data integrity and confidentiality, and for sender authentication and non-repudiation.
B's private · only B has it
One direction doesn't say who wrote

If we only encrypt with B's public key, confidentiality is guaranteed: nobody but B can read the message.

But there is a problem with authentication and non-repudiation: only a key that everyone knows was used to encrypt. Anyone could send a message pretending to be someone else.
The public key protects the content, but does not prove the sender's identity.
The impostor also has B's public key. The message arrives properly encrypted and B opens it without trouble, but has no way of knowing who wrote it.

The solution is to encrypt twice:

  • A encrypts the message with its private key and with B's public key.
  • B decrypts it with its private key and with A's public key.

Only B can open it, and only A could have produced it: we get confidentiality and, in addition, the possibility of authentication and non-repudiation.
A's private key proves who sent it; B's public key ensures only B reads it.
What A's public key opens could only have been locked by A's private key: authentication and non-repudiation.
What B's public key locks can only be opened by B's private key: confidentiality.

A hash function takes an input of arbitrary length and produces an output of fixed length: the digest. It must satisfy:

  • Consistency: the same input always gives the same output.
  • Randomness: prevents guessing the original message.
  • Uniqueness: it is practically impossible to find two messages with the same digest.
  • One way: given a digest, the input cannot be worked out.

They guarantee integrity. Examples: MD4, MD5, SHA.

A digital signature is an encrypted digest attached to a document.

The sender computes the hash of the document and encrypts that digest with their private key. The result, the signature, travels along with the document.

It can be used to confirm the sender's identity and to guarantee the integrity of the document.
Signature = hash of the document + encryption with the sender's private key.

The receiver separates the document from the signature and does two things:

  • Decrypts the signature with the sender's public key: obtains the original digest.
  • Computes the hash of the document received: obtains another digest.

Then it compares them. If they match, the document was not altered and the signature could only have been generated by the owner of the private key.
If they are equal: the document is intact and A signed it. If they differ: it was altered or it is not from A.

• Symmetric: one key, efficient; the problem is distributing it.
  • Asymmetric: public/private pair, more costly; data is encrypted with the recipient's public key.
  • Double encryption: adds authentication and non-repudiation.
  • Hash: fixed-length digest, guarantees integrity.
  • Digital signature: encrypted digest attached to the document.
